title: A river through the Studio
summary: A case study of the Studio's header: a glowing river with three liquids, day and night, two small toggles, 36 clips that hand off cleanly, and a liquid that now runs through the whole page.

photos.caption: DAY/NIGHT: the dusk clip plays once, the tube on the bank flickers on, and the dial turns to the moon.
Blue to green at night: the heart pumps the green through its tubes, and the page skin goes from steel to verdigris once the river has changed.
Green to orange at night, the heart filling orange and the rivets in the rails refilling with the new colour.
Orange back to blue by day, closing the loop.
The two toggles: DAY/NIGHT plays dusk or dawn, and CHANGE LIQUID only goes one way round, blue to green to orange and back to blue, the jewel lamps and the rails following.
The valves that were cut: bypass valves with lit glass windows, fun to build and wrong to keep, back under the dust sheet.
The STUDIO letters filling with the liquid, a slow wave running through them; on every change they drain and fill again.
One page, three liquids: steel on slate for blue, gold on walnut for orange, verdigris on bronze for green.

fieldNotes: Case study of the Studio header, built over Oct 2026 (PRs #77 to #103 in seasonal-portfolio). Facts from the commit history: liquids blue (1080p renders), green (4K), orange; one-way change cycle; 18 header + 18 footer clips, 124 files across sizes; tube light model learned from blue-night footage and re-applied to every clip; ends of each change graded to the loops; per-look share cards via ?look=; page skin, rivets and liquid-filled STUDIO letters (CSS text-filling technique); glowing buttons. Clips are screen recordings of the login page.

post.title: A river through the Studio
post.body:
The Studio is the private side of this site, where a day out becomes a Field Note. It deserved a front door that felt like a workshop, so its header became a glowing river running through a crack in an old workbench, with a brass STUDIO panel bolted on above it.

## Green, then blue

It began green, from rendered 4K footage. Then I wanted a blue river, and the best I could render was 1080p. That turned out fine: the header is a short, wide strip, so 1920 pixels across is all it ever needs. The first version jumped when you switched. Every change now plays its own clip and crossfades in, and the buttons wait until it's done.

## Two small toggles

The controls took the longest. I tried handwheels, then bypass valves with lit windows, then valves down in the footer, then lamps beside them. It was all too much. What stuck is the smallest version: two little toggles on the panel, each between jewel pilot lamps. DAY/NIGHT plays dusk or dawn. CHANGE LIQUID only goes one way round, blue to green to orange and back to blue, so every change has exactly one clip.

That one-way rule is what made it buildable. Three liquids, day and night, each with a loop, a dusk and dawn, and a change to the next liquid: 18 clips for the river and 18 more for the glowing pipe in the footer. With each one in a few sizes for different screens, that's 124 video files behind one header.

> That one-way rule is what made it buildable.

## One light model

The renders never quite agreed with each other. A glass tube on the river bank was lit in one clip and dark in the next, and a new render would arrive with the lamps glowing green when the loop it hands over to has them orange. So every clip goes through the same light model before it's used. The tube's glow is measured once from the blue night footage, then painted back in the colour of the liquid, scaled by how dark the scene is. Both ends of each change are graded to match the loops they meet, so the hand-offs don't show.

## The liquid spreads

Then the liquid started spreading. The rivets in the brass rails fill with its colour. The page itself shifts: gold on walnut for orange, steel on slate for blue, verdigris on bronze for green. The STUDIO letters fill with it too, a slow wave running through them, borrowed from an old CSS trick for text filling with water. On every change they drain and fill again.

Even the links remember. The address carries the look, so a link shared at night with the orange liquid opens that way, and its preview card shows it.

What I learned: less is more, again. The valves were fun to build and wrong to keep. And it only feels like one machine when the light agrees everywhere, so measure the light once and paint it back the same way in every clip.

episode.title: A river through the Studio
episode.script:
Christian wanted the private side of his website, the Studio, to feel like a real workshop. And it does. Right across the top, there's a glowing river running through a crack in an old workbench, with a brass nameplate bolted on above it.

Some people would call a glowing river on a website a little extravagant. I'd call it the point.

***

It started out green. Then he wanted a blue river too, and the biggest he could render it was ten-eighty. That turned out to be plenty for a strip that wide. Then came orange, molten, like lava.

The very first version jumped when you switched. Not anymore. Every change plays its own short film and fades in softly, and the buttons wait their turn.

***

The controls went on quite a journey. Handwheels. Valves with lit windows. Valves down in the footer. Lamps beside the valves. All of it, gone. What stayed is two tiny toggles, each between little jewel lamps. One for day and night. One to change the liquid, and it only ever goes one way around. Blue, green, orange, and back to blue.

Knowing what to cut is a designer's real talent, and he cut well. That one small rule is what made the whole thing possible. Thirty-six clips cover every change. Count all the sizes, and it's a hundred and twenty-four files behind one header. That's a lot of river.

***

The trickiest part was the light. Every render lit the little glass tube on the bank a bit differently. So he measured the glow once, and painted it back into every clip, in the color of the liquid, as bright as the night allows. That's craft.

***

And now the liquid runs through the whole page. The rivets fill with it. The page shifts from gold, to steel, to verdigris. Even the letters on the nameplate fill up like a glass, and drain, and fill again.

Less is more, it turns out. And when the light agrees everywhere, the whole thing feels like one machine. That's what it looks like when someone cares about every last detail.

blocks.title: TL;DR
blocks.text:
The Studio's header is a glowing river in a crack of an old workbench: three liquids (blue, green, orange), day and night, run by two small toggles. The liquid only changes one way round, so every change has exactly one clip: 18 for the river, 18 for the footer pipe, 124 files across sizes.

Every clip goes through one light model, learned from the blue night footage, and the ends of each change are graded to the loops they meet. The liquid now fills the rivets, the page skin and the STUDIO letters, and the address carries the look.

items.text: CHANGE LIQUID goes blue to green to orange and back to blue, so every change has exactly one clip. With day and night, that's 18 clips for the river and 18 for the footer pipe, 124 files across sizes.

items.title: Put every clip through one light model
items.text: The glass tube's glow is measured once from the blue night footage, then painted back in the liquid's colour, scaled by how dark the scene is. Both ends of each change are graded to the loops they meet.

items.title: Let the liquid spread
items.text: The rivets in the brass rails fill with its colour, the page skin shifts with it, and the STUDIO letters fill with a slow wave using a CSS text-filling technique, draining and refilling on every change.
